item.title: New Species of Cat Discovered for First Time in a Century
item.description: The species, called a tilcayo, is smaller than a house cat and lives in the cloud forests of the Andes Mountains in Bolivia.
item.dc:creator: Kate Golembiewski

item.title: Will A.I. Kill Us? Can It Hack My Bank Account? Your A.I. Questions Answered
item.description: Nearly 1,000 readers sent us their questions about artificial intelligence, its potential and its potential risks.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz, Dylan Freedman and K. R. Callaway
item.media:credit: Charles Taylor/Alamy
item.media:description: Some people worry that connecting A.I. agents to the internet or vital infrastructure will wreak havoc in unexpected ways, while others worry that researchers will soon develop A.I. systems that have agency.

item.title: NASA Telescope Helps Scientists Find a New Type of X-ray Object
item.description: The discovery of “hypersoft” X-ray beacons could help solve some mysteries about the universe.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang
item.media:credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/Univ. of Alabama/M. Muhibullah et al.; Optical: NASA/ESA/STScI; Image Processing: NASA/CXC/SAO/N. Wolk

item.title: This Rare Gene Drastically Raises Lung Cancer Risk in People Who Never Smoked
item.description: The gene is found predominantly in Southern Appalachia and may be one of the most powerful cancer-risk mutations ever found.
item.dc:creator: Gina Kolata
item.media:credit: Annie Flanagan for The New York Times
item.media:description: Caroline Blanchard, a nurse practitioner in New Orleans, has the lung cancer gene, known as EGFR T790M. One in 15,000 people in the United States have it.

item.title: What Happens When A.I. Stops Doing What Humans Want?
item.description: “Alignment” is the science of teaching A.I. to do what is in line with human preferences, ethics and judgment. But, at times, the systems have gone rogue.
item.dc:creator: Dylan Freedman
item.media:credit: Gabby Jones/Bloomberg
item.media:description: When an A.I. system starts acting of its own accord, engages in unsafe behavior or ignores the wishes of humans, the behavior is known as misalignment.

item.title: The Next Gene-Editing Technology May Also Be the Oldest
item.description: Scientists have discovered a powerful gene-targeting system in viruses. Billions of years old, VIPR seems to predate CRISPR and may be even more effective.
item.dc:creator: Carl Zimmer

item.title: A Feather Found in Dinosaur Poop Might Explain How Birds Beat Extinction
item.description: It’s the only example of a dinosaur-era feather found within rock that wasn’t completely flattened through the centuries.
item.dc:creator: K. R. Callaway

item.title: Scientists Overhaul Giant Particle Collider in Search of Universe’s Hidden Building Blocks
item.description: The European Organization for Nuclear Research, or CERN, will dismantle the Large Hadron Collider, which helped discover the so-called God Particle, in order to build a more powerful particle accelerator.
item.dc:creator: K. R. Callaway

item.title: Microscopic Videos That Show the Invisible Wonders Around Us
item.description: The winners of this year’s Nikon Small World in Motion competition showcase the wiggly, feathery, undulating beauty of invisible life.
item.dc:creator: Stella Raine Chu

item.title: Creating a Kill Switch to Shut Down a Rogue A.I. Is Harder Than It Sounds
item.description: A bipartisan group in Congress and Gov. Gavin Newsom of California have floated ideas for building a mechanism that would instantly power down an A.I. system. Only no one really knows how.
item.dc:creator: Dylan Freedman and Dustin Volz
item.media:credit: Tom Fox/The Dallas Morning News, via Getty Images
item.media:description: Creating a kill switch, a metaphorical big red button that could be pressed in an emergency, is harder than many policymakers assume. “There often isn’t one plug you can pull,” said one A.I. researcher.

item.title: How Trump Has Disrupted National Parks
item.description: Maintenance projects have been put off around the country and resources diverted to the president’s favored projects in Washington.
item.dc:creator: Maxine Joselow
item.media:credit: Erin Schaff/The New York Times
item.media:description: An unstaffed entrance station at Zion National Park in Utah.

item.title: Video Shows a San Diego Dog Seeming to Greet an Intruder. Why Didn’t He Bark?
item.description: Dog behavior experts offered a variety of explanations for why Nash the golden retriever wagged his tail and carried a toy near a man who broke into his owner’s home.
item.dc:creator: Michael Levenson

item.title: Toxic Fracking Waste Becoming a Political Issue in Ohio
item.description: The Democratic candidate for governor backed restrictions on disposal of fracking wastewater around a hard-hit town, and called for a “thorough investigation” of the dangers.
item.dc:creator: Quinn Glabicki
item.media:credit: Maddie McGarvey for The New York Times
item.media:description: Ohio has become a destination for the underground disposal of fracking wastewater, much of it from nearby Pennsylvania. In Ohio, it is damaging some natural-gas wells.

item.title: Human-Caused Warming Played ‘Very Strong’ Role in Himalayan Floods, Report Finds
item.description: Rising temperatures contributed to the disaster by destabilizing the permafrost and ice around the collapsed rock, scientists concluded.
item.dc:creator: Raymond Zhong
item.media:credit: Atul Loke for The New York Times
item.media:description: The widened channel of the Bhote Koshi River in Nepal after the flash flooding last month.

item.title: Trump Administration Moves to Gut a Core Endangered Species Protection
item.description: An internal memo reinterprets the law so that only the intentional killing of animals, not collateral harm, is illegal.
item.dc:creator: Catrin Einhorn
item.media:credit: Robert F. Bukaty/Associated Press, photographed under NOAA permit # 21371
item.media:description: A North Atlantic right whale off Cape Cod, Mass., in 2023. Only about 380 remain on the planet.

item.title: Fiji Declares a National Emergency as H.I.V. Cases Skyrocket
item.description: Surging drug use has contributed to an epidemic in the Pacific island nation, where one in 60 adults is estimated to be living with the virus.
item.dc:creator: Zane Irwin
item.media:credit: Agence France-Presse — Getty Images
item.media:description: An H.I.V. awareness poster displayed in Suva, Fiji, in April. The nation recorded more than 2,000 new cases in 2025, 16 times as many as in 2019, officials said.

item.title: T. Rex, King of the Dinosaurs, Had a Body Temperature of 97 Degrees
item.description: Hotter than a crocodile, cooler than a chicken, T. Rex was definitely warm-blooded, according to a new study.
item.dc:creator: Carolyn Y. Johnson

item.title: Massive Black Holes May Have Started as Little Red Dots
item.description: A new simulation suggests little red dots, unusually compact objects seen in photos from space, might be one stage in the evolution of black holes.
item.dc:creator: K. R. Callaway
item.media:credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, V. Kokorev (University of Texas at Austin), A. Pagan (STScI)
item.media:description: So-called little red dots, astronomical objects that date back about a billion years after the Big Bang, may be precursors to black holes, a new study has found.

item.title: Rising Seas Are Gobbling Up Beaches Around the World. A.I. Might Restore Them.
item.description: An experiment with roots at M.I.T. used A.I. and satellite images to grow a coastline in the Maldives. More projects are planned for Boston and Miami.
item.dc:creator: Quinn Glabicki

item.title: These Mice Have Partly Human Brains
item.description: The animals may help reveal the causes of brain disease in people and point the way to treatments. But researchers already are calling for new ethical guidelines.
item.dc:creator: Carl Zimmer and Carolyn Y. Johnson

item.title: The Liftoff Scenario That Terrifies A.I. Doomsayers
item.description: “Recursive self-improvement” is the idea that artificial intelligence could learn to build and train itself, creating exponential new progress — and risk.
item.dc:creator: Cade Metz
item.media:credit: Alana Paterson for The New York Times
item.media:description: Jeff Clune a computer scientist and researcher at the University of British Columbia in Canada and founder of Recursive Superintelligence, one of two $4-billion start-ups chasing recursive self-intelligence.

item.title: Mothers’ Intrusive Thoughts Are Mostly Benign. Lindsay Clancy’s Case Is an Exception.
item.description: Experts say that after childbirth, intrusive thoughts are common and mostly benign. Lindsay Clancy’s story provides a disturbing exception.
item.dc:creator: Ellen Barry
item.media:credit: Pool photo by Greg Derr

item.title: Does This Bird’s Return to Britain Restore History or Rewrite It?
item.description: Conservationists set up a colony of white storks in southern England, touching off a debate over whether they truly belong there.
item.dc:creator: Leo Sands and Hannah Reyes Morales
item.media:credit: Hannah Reyes Morales for The New York Times

item.title: Is There Anything Google’s Fruit Fly Brain Can’t Do?
item.description: Models of the insect’s nervous system have been trained to solve a Rubik’s Cube, play video games and even parallel park a car.
item.dc:creator: Michael Levenson

item.title: A T. Rex Walked Here: Teacher Finds Rare Footprints in North Dakota
item.description: Kent Hups, a high school science teacher in Colorado, discovered a 23-foot trackway of fossilized dinosaur footprints, which offer a glimpse of how the apex predator moved 66 million years ago.
item.dc:creator: Adeel Hassan
item.category: Denver Museum of Nature and Science

item.title: Disaster Survivors Sticking Together

item.media:description: Debris from a home destroyed in the Eaton fire in Altadena, Calif., in 2025.

item.title: Harold Freeman, Who Helped Remove Barriers to Cancer Treatment, Dies at 93
item.description: He developed a program that became a model for hospitals around the world, making it easier for poor Black patients to navigate an onerous bureaucratic system.
item.dc:creator: Richard Sandomir
item.category: Lauren, Ralph, Center for Cancer Care and Prevention
item.media:credit: Frances Roberts for The New York Times
item.media:description: Harold Freeman in 2000. Early in his career as a surgeon, he said, he thought he could “cut cancer out of Harlem,” but he soon learned that “the disease would not yield to a surgeon’s knife.”

item.title: FEMA Could Still Lose More Jobs Despite Court Ruling

item.dc:creator: Scott Dance

item.title: Exoplanets Offer Clues to What Lies Beyond Our Solar System
item.description: Thousands of planets have been discovered beyond our solar system, offering clues to where life might thrive and whether Earth is truly unique.
item.dc:creator: Natalie Wolchover

item.title: A.I. Queries From Abroad Raise Fears of a Biological Weapons Race

item.title: As Millions of Birds Migrate, Residents Are Asked to Turn Off the Lights
item.description: Birds are drawn to lights, and more than a billion die each year after crashing into buildings, experts said.
item.dc:creator: Ishani Desai

item.media:description: Birds fill the sky over Ohio in 2025. Tens of millions of migratory birds are expected to take flight Saturday across the Midwest.
